catalog_quote: STRESS The stress system of Ojibwe has been analyzed by a number of researchers (Bloomfield 1958, Rhodes 1976, Valentine 1985, etc.). Basically, the system is one of quantity sensitive iambic feet built from the left edge of the word, i.e., a preferred rhythm of weak-strong, in which the weak position m a y only be filled by a short vowel. The final syllable is often analyzed as extrametrical. ... In other dialects, such as Berens River Ojibwe, the same quantity-sensitive iambic metrical patterns are evident, but the correlate of stress in these dialects is pitch, resulting in alternations of high and low tones on stressed and unstressed vowels (see Fiero 1964, Valentine 1987). ... The stress system of northern dialects remains to be worked out, though m u c h information can be found in Valentine (1994) ... readall_conflicts: Surface disagreement only. Baraga 1878 (pp. 5-6) presents the accent as placed on the syllable 'pronounced with more emphasis or stress than the others', gives no positional rule, and says moving it 'sometimes entirely changes the meaning of the word' (ânakwad 'cloudy' / anâkan 'mat'; sâgaigan 'small lake' / sagâigan 'nail'; nibîng 'in the water' / nîbing 'in summer'), which read literally is lexical, unpredictable stress and would contradict the catalog's quantity-sensitive iambic rule (Valentine 1996 pp. 312-314; Swierzbin 2003). But each pair differs in vowel length, not in stress placement on equal syllables, and the 1878 editors state (Remarks on this second edition, p. [ix]) that the accents mark 'the vowels to be pronounced long or emphatically'; Remark 7 (p. 112) likewise says the accented 1sg conjunct ending 'is pronounced long' and the unaccented 2sg 'is very short'. Baraga's accent thus marks the heavy syllable, which is where the catalog's rule places stress, so the data agree and only the 19th-century analysis differs. the catalog reading stands unchanged.

sources.note: The catalog record for nort2961 (Valentine 1996 pp. 312-314 + Swierzbin 2003) is quantity-sensitive left-to-right iambic feet with every long vowel heading a foot. Baraga states no rule and on its face treats accent placement as meaning-distinguishing, but every one of his nine examples on p. 6 and the 1sg/2sg and excl/incl endings on pp. 111-112 differ by vowel length (aanakwad/anaakan, zaaga'igan/zagaa'igan, nibiing/niibing; -yaan vs -yan, -yaang vs -yang), and the 1878 editors say outright that the accents mark vowels 'to be pronounced long or emphatically'.
